title: The five, the four, the forty
hookLine: it remembers the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty liberated

cards: Three numbers. Say them fast and they sound like a phone number: five, four, forty. Each one is a group of people.
One group stepped forward when everyone else stepped back. One was four brothers, two of them still small boys. One walked away from their Guru, and then came back.
The Ardas says all three numbers in a single breath, right after the Guru Granth Sahib, before any other Sikhs it remembers.

teach.b: The line goes: panjaan piaariaan, chauhaan sahibzaadiaan, chaaleeaan mukteaan. The five beloved, the four princes, the forty liberated. The five are the Panj Pyare.
At Vaisakhi at Anandpur, Sikh tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh stood before a huge gathering with a sword and asked for someone willing to give their head. A long silence. Then one man stood.
Then four more. As the story is told, they came from different castes and regions: a shopkeeper, a farmer, a water carrier, a washerman, a barber.
They were the first initiated into the Khalsa, and Sikhs say the Guru then asked them to initiate him. Ever since, five initiated Sikhs lead the amrit ceremony.
The four are the Sahibzade, the Guru's sons. The older two, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, died fighting at Chamkaur.
The younger two, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, still small boys, were captured and executed at Sirhind after, tradition says, refusing to give up their faith. Sikhs mark their martyrdom every year.
The forty are the Chali Mukte.
During the siege of Anandpur, a group of Sikhs left the Guru and, tradition says, signed a paper disowning him. At home they were shamed for it, and a woman named Mai Bhago led them back.
They fought at Khidrana, now Muktsar, and fell. As the last of them lay dying, the story goes, the Guru tore up the paper. That's why they're called mukte, the liberated.
Five who stepped forward, four who held on, forty who came back: Sikhs hear in them three ways a person can be faithful.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty Muktas in one line; five initiated Sikhs still lead every amrit ceremony, and the Sahibzade's martyrdom is marked each year.

o: the Panj Pyare, first five of the Khalsa
the first five Gurus, Nanak to Arjan
five saints whose hymns open the scripture

games.q: the five, the four, the forty — tap the pairs.

s: the Panj Pyare all came from the same caste
they came from different castes and regions.
the forty are called mukte, the liberated, because the Guru tore up their paper
as the last of them died, the story says.
the two younger Sahibzade died fighting at Chamkaur
the older two fell at Chamkaur; the younger two were executed at Sirhind.

games.q: Vaisakhi at Anandpur. the Guru stands with a sword and asks for someone willing to give their head. the crowd is silent. what does tradition say happened?
o: nobody answered and he put the sword away.
one man stood, then four more.
the whole crowd stood at once.
games.why: one by one, five stood. they became the Panj Pyare, the first of the Khalsa, and Sikhs say the Guru then asked them to initiate him.

practice: On one out-breath, say five, and picture people standing up in a silent crowd; on the next, four, and picture four brothers, two grown and two small; on the next, forty, people walking back toward someone they'd left.
Repeat it slowly, and notice which you understand best right now: stepping forward, holding on, or coming back. If you pray, follow with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: The five. The Panj Pyare who stood up, the four Sahibzade, and the forty who came back: remembered in one breath.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, first initiated into the Khalsa.

carryVoice: Your line: five, four, forty. Three numbers, three groups, said in one breath. That's day six hundred twenty-one.
